name: Journey to the West
info: Journey to the West is a Chinese novel of the Ming dynasty, attributed to Wu Cheng'en, that turns the monk Xuanzang's 7th-century pilgrimage to India into a fantastic adventure led by the Monkey King, Sun Wukong.

facts.made: Traditionally ascribed to Wu Cheng'en, though much of its material came from older folk tales and storytelling; Wu is generally accepted as the author of the 1592 printed version
facts.form: A Chinese novel of 100 chapters in four unequal parts, mixing prose with poems and songs, written in the 16th century during the Ming dynasty
facts.where: Read in printed editions and in translations; the earliest surviving edition was printed at Nanjing in 1592
facts.known: Sun Wukong, the Monkey King; the pilgrimage of Tang Sanzang to India; Zhu Bajie and Sha Wujing; the 81 tribulations; the Ring Tightening Mantra; Waley's Monkey

t: The novel retells the real journey of the monk Xuanzang, who left Chang'an in 629, as a fantasy in which demons, immortals and a monkey who rebelled against Heaven escort a pilgrim to India.
Its stories circulated in oral storytelling for centuries before the 100-chapter form of the 16th century, and its authorship is still disputed, though Wu Cheng'en is traditionally named.
It has been read as a comic adventure, a satire of Chinese bureaucracy, a source of spiritual reflection and an allegory, and it reached English readers through Arthur Waley's abridgement of 1942.
dyk: Sun Wukong's staff weighs 17,550 pounds (7,960 kg) in the novel. It began as a pillar supporting the undersea palace of the Dragon King of the East Sea, and he can shrink it to the size of a needle and keep it in his ear.
ev: The monk Xuanzang leaves Chang'an for India in defiance of Emperor Taizong's ban on travel
During the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279), embellished stories based on Xuanzang's journey appear in book form
The Yongle Encyclopedia is completed, holding excerpts of a version of the story in colloquial Chinese
The earliest surviving edition of the novel is published at Nanjing
Dong Yue writes the satirical sequel Xiyoubu, set between chapters 61 and 62
Arthur Waley publishes Monkey, an abridged English translation of 30 of the 100 chapters
Anthony C. Yu begins publishing the first complete English translation to render the poems and songs, finished in 1983

sections.origins:
The novel rests on a real journey. The monk Xuanzang (602–664), of Jingtu Temple in the capital Chang'an, left in 629, in defiance of Emperor Taizong of Tang's ban on travel, to seek Buddhist scriptures in India. Helped by sympathetic Buddhists, he went through Gansu and Qinghai to Kumul and Turpan, then across regions that are today Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Afghanistan into Gandhara. He travelled through India for the next thirteen years, visited Buddhist pilgrimage sites and studied at the university at Nalanda. He left India in 643 and reached Chang'an in 646, where Taizong welcomed him.

Embellished stories based on the journey had circulated in China through oral storytelling for centuries. They appeared in book form as early as the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279), and the Yongle Encyclopedia, completed in 1408, contains excerpts of a version in colloquial Chinese. The plot was also part of folk and literary tradition as folk stories in informal language, a poetic novelette and a six-part drama series. Of an earlier text, Journey to the West as Storytelling, only fragments survive in other texts, among them the wager between the Dragon King of the Jing River and the fortune teller Yuan Shoucheng.
sections.content:
The novel has 100 chapters in four unequal parts. The first, chapters 1 to 7, is a self-contained prologue on Sun Wukong, a monkey born from a stone egg on Flower Fruit Mountain. He learns the Tao, 72 transformations and the secrets of immortality, takes the title Great Sage Equal to Heaven and rebels against Heaven, until the Buddha traps him under a mountain for 500 years. Chapters 8 to 12 introduce Tang Sanzang and how Emperor Taizong sends him west, at the Buddha's instruction to the bodhisattva Guanyin to find someone in China to bring the sutras back.

The third part, chapters 13 to 99, is an episodic adventure. Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing and the White Dragon Horse accompany Tang Sanzang, atoning for earlier sins, and fend off demons and animal spirits, many of whom want to eat his flesh, which was believed to give immortality. The geography is almost entirely fantasy. The travellers face 81 tribulations, and at length Tang Sanzang receives the scriptures from the living Buddha at Vulture Peak. In chapter 100 they return to the Tang empire and are rewarded: Sun Wukong and Tang Sanzang reach Buddhahood, Sha Wujing becomes an arhat, the White Dragon Horse a naga, and Zhu Bajie an altar cleanser.
sections.making:
The modern 100-chapter form of the novel dates from the 16th century. The earliest surviving edition was published in 1592 in Nanjing. Two earlier editions appeared between 1522 and 1566, but no copies of them survive. Authorship is traditionally ascribed to Wu Cheng'en, and the question is complicated because much of the material came from folk tales. Anthony C. Yu, writing in 2012, said that the dispute over authorship had see-sawed for nearly a century without resolution.

Hu Shih wrote in 1942 that the people of Wu's hometown had attributed the novel to him early and kept records to that effect as early as 1625. David Lattimore replied in 1983 that the gazetteer says only that Wu wrote something called The Journey to the West, and mentions no novel. W. J. F. Jenner observed that the novel contains no political detail that a fairly well-read commoner could not have known. One interpretive tradition sees the book as the outcome of a writing game popular among Chinese literati. The cumulative authorship is acknowledged, but Wu is generally accepted as the author of the 1592 printed version, which is widely considered canonical.
sections.reception:
The novel is regarded as one of the great Chinese novels and has been described as arguably the most popular literary work in East Asia. It is at once a comic adventure, a satire of Chinese bureaucracy, a source of spiritual reflection and a rich allegory. In the story Sun Wukong stands for the human mind and impulse, the so-called monkey mind, Tang Sanzang for the human heart, Zhu Bajie for base human nature, Sha Wujing for obedience and conformity without thought, and the White Dragon Horse for the human will.

Interpretation has been disputed. Hu Shi, whose introduction to the 1943 edition of Waley's translation scorned the allegorical readings made popular in the Qing dynasty as old-fashioned, insisted that the stories were simply comic. Andrew H. Plaks writes that Waley's selection of episodes followed Hu Shi's lead and gave the misleading impression of a compendium of popular materials marked by folk wit and humour. Recent scholars in China and the West have shown levels of meaning and a looser allegorical framework that Hu Shi's reading does not account for.
sections.survival:
The text survives in printed editions rather than in any original manuscript. The earliest surviving edition is that of 1592, published at Nanjing, and the two earlier editions of 1522 to 1566 are lost. Of the earlier storytelling text only fragments are preserved in other works, and the surviving narrative threads include the wager of the Dragon King of the Jing River and the contest in Cart Slow Kingdom between the pilgrims and three Taoist demons.

The work passed to English readers through translation. Arthur Waley's abridged Monkey of 1942 was for many years the best-known version. It translated 30 of the 100 chapters, roughly a sixth of the whole, and left out most of the verse, which led one recent critic to rank it as a good retelling. Others have praised it as remarkably faithful to the original spirit. Anthony C. Yu's four-volume translation of 1977 to 1983 was the first to render the poems and songs, which he argues are essential to the author's meaning, and the University of Chicago Press issued a revised edition in 2012. W. J. F. Jenner's four volumes of 1982 to 1984 give a readable version without scholarly apparatus. Julia Lovell's selection appeared in 2021.
sections.legacy:
The novel has roots in Chinese folk religion, mythology, Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoist and Buddhist folklore, and its pantheon of Taoist immortals and Buddhist bodhisattvas still reflects certain Chinese religious attitudes. Many of its religious references involve plays on the names of characters and places that are often lost in translation. It is a progenitor of the xianxia genre, which combines martial arts with high fantasy, and has inspired many manhwa, manhua, manga and anime series.

Sequels began to appear in the late Ming and continued into the Qing dynasty and the modern period. One of the best regarded is Dong Yue's satirical Xiyoubu of about 1640, in which Sun Wukong is trapped in a dream world created by the Qing Fish Demon, the embodiment of desire. Dong wanted an opponent that Sun could not defeat with his strength and martial skill. The story has also been adapted for television in Japan and China, for the stage as operas by Fred Ho and Anna Vienna Ho, and for many other media.

summary: Journey to the West is a Ming-dynasty Chinese novel, attributed to Wu Cheng'en, that turns the monk Xuanzang's pilgrimage to India into a fantasy led by the Monkey King. Its earliest surviving edition dates from 1592, and its authorship is still debated.
references: James S. Fu, Mythic and Comic Aspects of the Quest (Singapore University Press, 1977)
